alternative: a runtime state machine - AASM or state_machines declaring states, events, transitions and guards, or the hand-written State pattern - since no Ruby construct can make an illegal transition fail before the program runs.
idiom_name: none at compile time; AASM / state_machines runtime state machine
implementation_notes: Ruby has no compile-time type parameters and no static checking, so the half of the pattern that puts the state in the type does not exist; what Ruby has is a mature runtime answer. Gems such as AASM and state_machines declare states, events, transitions and guards on the class, and an event fired from the wrong state is rejected (AASM raises InvalidTransition, or returns false in its non-whiny mode). The hand-written classic form is the State pattern - one class per state delegating behaviour - which gives state-specific methods but still checks every transition at run time.
code_sketch:
class Order
  include AASM
  aasm do
    state :pending, initial: true
    state :paid
    event :pay do
      transitions from: :pending, to: :paid
    end
  end
end
# order.pay! raises AASM::InvalidTransition while the order is not pending
pitfalls: Guards and validations run only at call time; a path that lacks a test simply goes undetected.
send, method_missing and direct instance-variable writes bypass the declared API, so the state machine cannot serve as a security boundary.
Workflows spanning several persisted columns drift out of sync; when concurrency matters guard transitions with a compare-and-swap update and an append-only log rather than in-memory state.
